title: For the First Time, a Look at the Arctic Bobtail Squid in Its Natural Habitat
gist: Researchers using a remote camera captured the first-ever image of the Arctic bobtail squid (Rossia moelleri) in its natural habitat, in Kong Oscar Fjord in Northeast Greenland National Park, along with the species' egg clusters. The account is published in Polar Biology.

themes.theme: First in-habitat imaging of Rossia moelleri

insights.claim: The first image ever captured of the Arctic bobtail squid (Rossia moelleri) in its natural habitat was taken by researchers using a remote camera in Kong Oscar Fjord, Northeast Greenland National Park, with the account published in Polar Biology.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Remote camera platforms are still turning up firsts in polar deep water — the Arctic benthos remains largely unsurveyed as it opens to industrial interest.
insights.locator: This mesmerizing deep sea creature is the Arctic bobtail squid

insights.claim: The same imaging captured egg clusters of the Arctic bobtail squid, giving experts an unprecedented look at the life and reproduction of the cephalopod.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Reproductive-habitat data is the input baseline scientists need before any Arctic seabed disturbance can be assessed.
insights.locator: As an extra bonus, egg clusters from the squid

insights.claim: Species identification of the imaged Arctic bobtail squid relied on several signals including its morphology and the placement of its eggs on a hard substrate — in this case a sheltered fjord wall.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Behavioral and substrate cues supplement morphology when a specimen cannot be collected — the working method for non-invasive deep-sea ID.
insights.locator: A number of signals were used to identify the species
